h: वंदे मातरम् : देवदत्त पटनायक की टिप्पणी (अंग्रेज़ी मूल)
body: Vande Mataram may not be a Hindu song or an Indian song। I just realized it। Vande Mataram could refer to any country। Even China।
Maybe I am wrong। I am no Sanskrit expert। So we need Brahmins to confirm। But please read the song। Slowly। In Sanskrit। The way its loudest defenders never do।

Sujalam, suphalam, malayaja-shitalam, shasya-shyamalam। Good water, good fruit, a breeze cooled by the sandalwood of the Malaya hills, dark green with crops। These are resources: forests, minerals, for Baniyas to sell। Name the river। Bankim does not। No Ganga, no Yamuna, no Himalaya, no Vindhya। Tagore's Jana Gana Mana cannot stop naming things: Punjab, Sindhu, Gujarat, Maratha, Dravida, Utkala, Banga, Vindhya, Himachal, Yamuna, Ganga। It even names the "jana gana", the crowd of people। Vande Mataram names no people। Its Mata has no address। She could be anybody's mother।

Saptakoti-kantha-kala-kala-ninada-karale, fearsome with the roar of seven crore throats। Dvisaptakoti-bhujair-dhrita-kharakaravale, fourteen crore arms gripping sharp swords। Seven crore was roughly the population of the Bengal Presidency in the 1872 census। Not India। Bengal। So the only headcount in the national song is a Bengali headcount। Bankim's motherland is Bengal at best। At worst, Bangladesh.Bengal sits next door to China। Calcutta had a Chinatown। Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, Brahmin and deputy magistrate in the service of the Raj, wrote the song in the 1870s and slipped it into Anandamath in 1882. Did he eat noodles while writing it? We know he hated Muslims। But worked for Englishmen।

Then the weather report। Shubhra-jyotsna-pulakita-yaminim, nights thrilled by white moonlight। Phulla-kusumita-drumadala-shobhinim, glowing with trees in full bloom। Suhasinim, sumadhura-bhashinim, sweet-smiling, sweet-speaking। Sukhadam, varadam, giver of comfort, giver of boons.Stand at the Yamuna in Okhla in November and watch the toxic foam float past। Breathe Delhi at AQI 400 and call it malayaja-shitalam। Look for the forests of Bhimashankar and Hasdeo, or the Uttarakhand hillsides sliced open for four-lane roads। So the song describes some other country। A clean one। Blue skies, on demand, the way Beijing switched off its factories for the 2008 Olympics। One guess। Or maybe the Gujarati Olympics of the future?
As for the moonlit yamini ask the families sleeping beside the rubble of their bulldozed homes how pulakita the night feels।

Sumadhura-bhashini? Switch on prime time। Watch the Brahmin anchors yelling and screaming cockroach and congress, Pakistan and Bangladesh, and cunningly ignoring China, Ladakh, Manipur and Arunachal Pradesh।

The later stanza seals it। Tvam hi Durga dashapraharana-dharini, you are Durga, holder of ten weapons। Ten weapons on one body is a drone payload। Kamala kamala-dala-viharini, Lakshmi playing among lotus petals। Tara holds the blue utpala, and rows of Buddhas sit on lotuses from Dunhuang to the Longmen caves at Luoyang। Vani vidyadayini, speech, giver of learning। Vani travelled east with the Suvarnaprabhasa Sutra and became Biancaitian in China and Benzaiten in Japan। A goddess of the East Asian Buddhist shelf, sitting inside the national song।

Put it together। No Indian river, no Indian mountain, no Indian people, a Bengal-sized census, Buddhist lotuses, a Sino-Japanese Saraswati, Chinatown down the road and a novel that bows to the British। Those who demand every student sing it or leave for Pakistan are not demanding loyalty to India। They are demanding loyalty to the country Bankim imagined, and it does not look like ours।
